responses.strategic_rationale: Denmark's digital identity system is structurally locked into Apple and Google's platform integrity signals, app-distribution controls, and device-trust models—a dependency that contradicts the national 2026–2029 digital-sovereignty mandate and creates single-point-of-failure risk for essential public services. The core tension is between the conservative, certification-heavy incumbent (MitID) and the need for institutional change before the new eIDAS2 wallet (AltID) hardens the same dependencies. The selected levers navigate this by combining technical credibility (demonstrators that prove standards-based alternatives are feasible), institutional leverage (formal engagement with Digitaliseringsstyrelsen and procurement gatekeepers), coalition pressure (civil-society and academic voices that reframe the issue as resilience, not disruption), and EU-level standards alignment (anchoring Danish advocacy in broader European interoperability mandates). These levers collectively make supplier-neutrality and fallback access harder to dismiss as ideological rather than operationally necessary.

levers.name: Demonstrator Scope and Fidelity
levers.consequences: Building working (but non-production) authenticators using FIDO2 and OpenID Connect on GrapheneOS proves that secure, standards-based, Apple/Google-independent authentication is technically feasible without requiring proprietary platform APIs. This lowers the perceived risk for procurement officials and standards bodies considering fallback requirements. The trade-off is that demonstrators do not integrate with live MitID or real public-sector identity providers, so they do not prove end-to-end operational compatibility or resolve all integration friction that would emerge at scale.
options: Develop two parallel demonstrators: one mobile-oriented (GrapheneOS or comparable platform running FIDO2/OpenID Connect) and one browser-based or hardware-token-based path that eliminates mobile-OS dependency altogether, each authenticated against a simulated Danish public-sector identity environment with published architecture documentation.

Focus demonstrator effort on a single, heavily polished mobile authenticator running on GrapheneOS that closely mirrors MitID's user interaction model and security posture, aiming for near-production-grade code quality and formal security review to maximize institutional credibility.

Pursue a lightweight proof-of-concept using existing open-source authentication libraries (e.g., Keycloak with FIDO2 modules) integrated with a mock identity provider, prioritizing speed to demonstration over custom development and accepting lower fidelity in exchange for faster iteration and lower technical risk.
levers.review_lever: A more sophisticated demonstrator improves institutional buy-in but risks scope creep and diverts engineering effort from policy leverage; a minimal proof-of-concept spreads resources thinly across coalition-building but may be dismissed as too academic or immature for procurement relevance.

levers.name: Institutional Entry Point and Engagement Strategy
levers.consequences: Engaging formally with Digitaliseringsstyrelsen, the MitID operator, or a regulatory body creates a documented commitment point and forces officials to provide written responses that either endorse platform-neutral requirements or articulate explicit resistance (which the project can then address). Early formal engagement builds credibility and creates institutional friction against backsliding. The risk is that incumbent operators or existing MitID stakeholders may actively undermine the project or lobby against platform-neutrality language, and early engagement can also prompt defensive institutional posturing if framed as a direct threat to existing investments.
options: Target Digitaliseringsstyrelsen directly with a formal written proposal framed around digital sovereignty and procurement neutrality, requesting an official steering-committee role or monthly update briefing to ensure the project shapes AltID design from the inside rather than remaining external pressure.

Approach the Danish Data Protection Authority (Datatilsynet) with a request for a public statement on platform-neutrality and fallback-access implications for data minimization and GDPR compliance, using privacy framing to create institutional pressure that does not directly threaten the MitID operator.

Engage with a sympathetic municipality or regional health authority using demonstrators to pilot a fallback-capable authentication interface, creating operational proof and local political pressure for platform-neutral procurement requirements in subsequent contracts.
levers.review_lever: Direct steering-committee placement risks co-option or blocking by incumbents; privacy-authority framing deprioritizes resilience and sovereignty arguments; municipal pilots build bottom-up pressure but move slowly and may lack influence on national AltID architecture decisions.

levers.name: Coalition Composition and Messaging
levers.consequences: A coalition spanning civil-society organisations, privacy advocates, academic researchers, security experts, and sympathetic parliamentarians creates distributed political and institutional pressure that cannot be easily dismissed as a single vendor's interests or an ideological fringe position. Different coalition members amplify different messages: security researchers emphasize technical feasibility, privacy groups emphasize data minimization and democratic accountability, and continuity-planning stakeholders emphasize resilience and supplier concentration risk. The challenge is that coalitions dilute focus and can become platforms for diverse agendas that weaken the core message around platform neutrality and fallback access.
options: Build a broad coalition including civil-society organisations, academic institutions, and EU-facing standards bodies (e.g., ETSI working groups), with explicit messaging discipline ensuring all members emphasize digital sovereignty, resilience, and reduced supplier concentration as primary drivers rather than secondary privacy or ideological concerns.

Form a narrower, technically credible coalition of security researchers and compliance experts with direct links to academic and industry standards bodies, positioning the project as a technical standards initiative rather than a political movement and accepting lower civil-society visibility in exchange for institutional weight.

Develop separate, audience-specific coalitions: a technical working group for standards bodies and procurement officials, a privacy-and-democracy coalition for civil-society and media engagement, and a parliamentary task force for political leverage, each with distinct messaging tailored to institutional incentives and risk tolerances.
levers.review_lever: Broad coalition maximizes political pressure but risks diluted messaging and slower consensus-building; narrow technical credibility improves standards traction but limits political cover if incumbents attack the project; segmented coalitions require sustained coordination overhead and may create contradictory external narratives.

levers.name: Feasibility Report Content and Publication Strategy
levers.consequences: A published feasibility and risk report that maps MitID dependencies, articulates platform-neutrality and fallback-access architecture options, and documents regulatory pathways under eIDAS2 and NSIS creates a citable reference document that procurement officials and standards bodies must address explicitly rather than ignore. Publication also distributes the project's analysis across European digital identity policy networks, raising the cost of dismissing supplier-concentration concerns as purely Danish or ideologically motivated. The trade-off is that a detailed technical report requires significant research and external review investment, and early publication may prompt defensive responses or lobbying from incumbent operators that accelerate opposition rather than convert skeptics.
options: Publish a comprehensive, externally reviewed feasibility and risk report (80–120 pages) covering architectural options, regulatory compliance pathways, supplier-concentration risks, and implementation timelines, with formal launch events at Digitaliseringsstyrelsen, EU technical working groups, and academic conferences to maximize institutional and media visibility.

Release a shorter, more accessible policy brief (15–25 pages) targeting procurement officials and parliamentarians, with detailed technical annexes available separately, prioritizing clarity and decision-maker accessibility over exhaustive coverage and aiming for faster dissemination and lower incumbent resistance.

Publish findings incrementally through academic conferences, EU standards working groups, and policy journals rather than a single consolidated report, spreading impact over time and reducing the visibility of a single confrontational document while allowing continuous refinement based on feedback.
levers.review_lever: Comprehensive publication maximizes institutional impact and creates a hard policy reference point, but also invites consolidated incumbent criticism and raises visibility to potential blockers; shorter briefs improve stakeholder accessibility but may be dismissed as insufficiently rigorous; incremental publication spreads impact but risks losing the coherence needed for procurement language adoption.

levers.name: EU-Level Standards Alignment and Negotiation
levers.consequences: Positioning Danish platform-neutrality and fallback-access arguments within the broader European Digital Identity Wallet (EUDI Wallet) framework and relevant eIDAS2 technical working groups anchors the project in supranational compliance and interoperability mandates rather than framing it as a Danish national preference. This creates pressure on Danish authorities to adopt requirements that align with EU-wide standards, reducing the risk that the project is dismissed as isolated or unilateral. The challenge is that EU-level engagement moves slowly, requires sustained diplomatic effort, and may be weakened by other Member States prioritizing incumbent operators or interoperability with existing national stacks.
options: Engage directly with ETSI, the EUDI Wallet technical working groups, and the European Commission's digital identity coordination structures to propose language supporting platform-neutral access and certified fallback mechanisms, positioning these as requirements for EU wallet interoperability rather than Danish-specific preferences.

Coordinate with sympathetic European Member States (e.g., Estonia, Netherlands) that share digital-sovereignty concerns to develop joint position papers and standards proposals, creating a broader coalition that makes dismissing platform-neutrality concerns harder for the Commission or other Member States.

Support the emergence of an independent European standards body or open-source authentication initiative that defines platform-neutral identity specifications, with Danish project demonstrators contributing proof-of-concept code and regulatory feedback to establish credible alternatives to Apple/Google-centric models.
levers.review_lever: Direct engagement with EU bodies improves long-term legitimacy but offers no guarantee of rapid policy change and may be viewed as premature by Danish stakeholders; multi-country coalitions amplify pressure but reduce Danish control over messaging; independent open-source standards bodies build technical credibility but take years to achieve institutional recognition.

levers.name: Fallback Access Path Definition and Use-Case Binding
levers.consequences: Defining a concrete, use-case-specific fallback authentication path (e.g., hardware-token-based, browser-based, or otherwise OS-agnostic) tied to critical services such as tax filing, healthcare access, or social-security claims demonstrates that resilience is not abstract but operationally necessary. This makes fallback access requirements harder to dismiss as optional or ideological. Defining use cases also forces procurement and architecture conversations to address what continuity of service actually means and what happens if the primary mobile-OS-dependent path fails. The trade-off is that narrowing fallback design to specific use cases reduces the universality of the solution and may invite incumbent pushback that fallback mechanisms should only apply to edge cases or geographic exceptions rather than core architectural requirements.
options: Specify a hardware-security-token-based fallback path (e.g., FIDO2-compatible USB or NFC tokens) usable for high-assurance transactions such as healthcare access and tax filing, ensuring it functions across all operating systems and does not depend on app-store distribution or platform integrity APIs.

Define a browser-based fallback using open standards (OpenID Connect with FIDO2 discoverable credentials) accessible from any device with a modern web browser, allowing citizens without specific mobile platforms to authenticate to public services without needing an iOS or Android app at all.

Establish a tiered resilience model where routine services rely on the current mobile-OS-dependent primary path, critical or time-sensitive services (emergency healthcare, benefits claims) trigger automatic fallback to a browser or hardware-token mechanism, and this tiering is formalized in AltID procurement and operational requirements.
levers.review_lever: Hardware tokens ensure OS independence but add cost, distribution burden, and user friction that may limit adoption; browser-based fallback reduces friction but may be perceived as lower-assurance and may struggle to achieve equivalent regulatory recognition; tiered resilience adds complexity to system design and procurement language but directly ties fallback mechanisms to demonstrated operational risk.

levers.name: Financing and Phase-Gate Risk Management
levers.consequences: Structuring the project into three phases with conditional funding (phases 2 and 3 contingent on phase 1 deliverables) ensures that the project does not commit large resources to downstream work if early institutional engagement fails or if the feasibility report reveals insurmountable blockers. This also creates natural decision points where the project can pivot toward EU-level standards input or coalition consolidation if Danish procurement leverage is weak. The challenge is that conditional funding creates uncertainty for the team, may discourage long-term staffing commitments, and may cause the project to lose momentum or miss windows of opportunity if phase gates are triggered before stakeholder engagement is sufficient.
options: Commit to full 10.5-million-DKK funding across all three phases upfront, treating phase gates as strategic checkpoints rather than hard funding barriers, ensuring team stability and allowing the project to pursue multiple intervention pathways simultaneously without artificial phase constraints interrupting momentum.

Implement strict phase-gate funding with transparent, publicly documented decision criteria, so that if phase 2 is not triggered due to insufficient institutional engagement, the project formally shifts to EU-level standards contribution and coalition consolidation, treating the strategic pivot as an acceptable outcome rather than a failure.

Secure parallel funding streams from EU digital-identity research programs, academic institutions, or civil-society networks, reducing dependence on the initial 10.5-million-DKK allocation and allowing phases to progress in parallel with lower inter-phase financial dependency.
levers.review_lever: Full upfront funding ensures team continuity but may waste resources if Danish procurement leverage does not materialize; strict phase gating enforces disciplined strategy but may trigger abandonment of Danish advocacy if metrics are met too early; parallel funding reduces risk but complicates governance and may dilute focus across multiple funders' priorities.

responses.strategic_rationale: Denmark faces a structural digital-sovereignty risk: essential public authentication for banking, tax, and healthcare depends on Apple and Google's platform-integrity signals and app-distribution controls, creating supplier concentration, contingency vulnerability, and reduced strategic autonomy. The project's core tension is between the conservative, certification-heavy MitID ecosystem (resistant to retrofitting) and the window of influence around AltID's eIDAS2 rollout (2026–2029). Success requires threading three competing needs: credible technical demonstration to overcome skepticism, coalition-building to shift political framing from ideological sovereignty to pragmatic resilience and continuity risk, and procurement language that embeds neutrality without triggering incumbent resistance or appearing to mandate immediate replacement. The selected levers address this by targeting demonstrator design (lean vs. feature-rich), coalition messaging (resilience vs. sovereignty), standards-body engagement (EU-level pressure vs. domestic focus), stakeholder sequencing (early wins with sympathetic authorities vs. frontal confrontation), and phase-gate gating (conditional release tied to institutional traction rather than technical completion alone).

levers.name: Demonstrator Positioning: Technical Proof Versus Political Signal
levers.consequences: Positioning the mobile and fallback demonstrators as narrow, non-production feasibility proofs rather than feature-complete alternatives reduces development scope and credibility risk, but may undermine their persuasiveness to procurement officials who expect to see operational maturity. Conversely, expanding them toward production readiness inflates budget, timeline, and certification complexity, potentially consuming the entire phase-two budget without achieving the advocacy goal.
options: Build minimal demonstrators (GrapheneOS + FIDO2 and a browser-based token fallback) deliberately constrained to three core authentication flows, with explicit documentation of what is intentionally omitted to remain within phase-two scope and budget.

Develop demonstrators with partial feature parity to MitID (multi-factor recovery, account linking, audit logging) to increase perceived credibility among technical reviewers, accepting a 15–20% budget increase and delayed delivery risk.

Partner with an existing open-source mobile identity project (e.g., a European eID wallet initiative) and contribute fallback-authentication modules rather than building demonstrators in-house, reducing isolation risk but accepting dependency on external project roadmaps.
levers.review_lever: Minimal scope preserves budget and timeline credibility, but narrow demonstrators may be dismissed as toys rather than evidence; feature expansion risks scope creep and budget overrun without guaranteeing procurement influence.

levers.name: Coalition Anchor Selection: Which Authority to Target First
levers.consequences: Early formal engagement with one sympathetic authority (e.g., the Data Protection Board or a parliamentary digital-policy committee member) creates institutional validation and media narrative momentum, but risks signaling a political stance that alienates other potential allies or triggers preemptive resistance from MitID operators. Sequencing toward multiple modest stakeholders instead spreads attention and reduces accusation of partisan coordination, but delays high-visibility wins and may dilute message clarity.
options: Target a single respected authority (e.g., the Datatilsynet or a senior Folketinget digital-policy member) for an early, publicly announced formal response or endorsement, accepting the political concentration risk in exchange for clear narrative momentum.

Build a broad coalition across civil-society organizations, academic institutions, and regional government bodies first, then present a collective position to Digitaliseringsstyrelsen, ensuring distributed legitimacy but delaying visible institutional traction until month 12–14.

Approach the MitID operator directly with a confidential proposal to collaborate on fallback pathways, framing it as strategic partnership rather than criticism, risking co-option but potentially converting the incumbent into a neutral or supportive voice.
levers.review_lever: Early single-authority wins create narrative credibility but concentrate political exposure; broad coalition building delays visible traction but disperses risk and reduces accusation of partisan pressure or incumbent capture.

levers.name: Resilience Framing Versus Sovereignty Language in Policy Messaging
levers.consequences: Emphasizing continuity-of-service, supplier-concentration, and contingency risk ('What if Apple or Google withdraw from Denmark?') appeals to risk managers and procurement officers but risks being perceived as alarmist or commercially motivated if competitors are suspected of backing the messaging. Framing as digital sovereignty and democratic control attracts civil-society and parliamentary support but triggers incumbent framing of the concern as ideological and expensive, and may activate EU-level free-trade sensitivities.
options: Lead messaging with resilience, contingency, and supplier-concentration risk (suppliers cannot simultaneously leave or be locked by geopolitical pressure), positioning fallback access as critical infrastructure continuity planning, de-emphasizing ideology.

Anchor messaging in democratic sovereignty and reduced dependence on foreign tech-platform policy decisions that affect Danish public-sector autonomy, accepting that this framing will trigger incumbent claims of expense and unrealism.

Dual-track messaging: resilience and contingency planning in procurement and risk-management forums; sovereignty and democratic control in parliamentary and civil-society contexts, with a unified technical brief explaining both framings as complementary rather than contradictory.
levers.review_lever: Resilience framing is operationally credible but may be dismissed as overblown; sovereignty framing mobilizes civil society but invites dismissal as ideologically driven; dual-track messaging increases coordination overhead and risks internal contradiction if not carefully managed.

levers.name: Stakeholder Sequencing: Sympathetic-First Versus Incumbent-Negotiation Approach
levers.consequences: Building momentum through early wins with sympathetic civil-society, academic, and parliamentary allies before formally engaging MitID operators or Digitaliseringsstyrelsen creates political weight and precedent, but risks being perceived as a coordinated campaign to exclude incumbents, triggering defensive mobilization and procurement delays. Direct early engagement with operators shows good faith and may uncover technical collaboration opportunities, but dilutes pressure and may result in assurances that deflect policy change without substantive action.
options: Secure published support from at least three independent civil-society and academic organizations and one parliamentary ally by month 6, establish the fallback-access concept in public discourse, then approach Digitaliseringsstyrelsen and the MitID operator from a position of demonstrated coalition strength.

Request formal technical working-group participation with the MitID operator and Digitaliseringsstyrelsen by month 3, treating them as co-designers rather than obstacles, accepting slower narrative momentum in exchange for insider access and potential collaborative problem-solving.

Parallel-path approach: simultaneously build civil-society coalition and initiate low-key technical discussions with sympathetic officials within Digitaliseringsstyrelsen or AltID governance, avoiding public confrontation until month 12 when demonstrators and coalition provide joint credibility.
levers.review_lever: Sympathetic-first approach builds political power but risks appearing coordinated or exclusionary; incumbent-first risks co-option or capture; parallel-path spreads resources and requires careful message discipline to avoid appearing duplicitous.

levers.name: EU-Level Standards Engagement Scope: Domestic Leverage Versus European Alignment
levers.consequences: Deep early engagement with European Digital Identity Wallet working groups and eIDAS2 implementation bodies amplifies the project's reach and aligns Danish advocacy with broader EU momentum on interoperability and resilience, but may slow phase-three domestic procurement impact if European alignment requires consensus-building across member states with different vendor relationships. Focusing first on Danish AltID procurement and then scaling to EU standards bodies preserves domestic momentum but risks missing the window for European-level language if eIDAS2 wallet implementation timelines are already set.
options: Engage with relevant EU technical working groups (eIDAS2 Wallet rollout, NSIS implementation) by month 8, propose platform-neutrality and fallback-access requirements at the EU level, positioning Denmark as a leader in resilience standards, accepting slower domestic impact if European buy-in is delayed.

Concentrate phase-three effort on AltID and Danish procurement language, treating EU engagement as secondary and deferred to month 18–20, preserving focus and budget for domestic institutional traction but risking missed leverage if European timelines accelerate.

Dual-track EU engagement: observe and participate in standards discussions from month 6 onward (low-intensity), then escalate to formal position papers and procurement-language proposals by month 14 once demonstrators and Danish institutional traction are visible, balancing European alignment with domestic credibility.
levers.review_lever: Early deep EU engagement amplifies reach but may slow domestic wins; domestic-first focus preserves clarity but risks European window closure; dual-track requires sustained coordination and risks appearing reactive at both levels if timing misaligns.

levers.name: Fallback-Access Design Governance: Standards-Based Versus Proprietary-Hybrid
levers.consequences: Committing the fallback demonstrator entirely to open standards (WebAuthn, OpenID Connect, FIDO2, hardware tokens) maximizes platform independence and procurement appeal, but reduces integration options with existing MitID infrastructure and may exclude approaches that leverage proprietary device-security features without full Apple/Google mediation. A hybrid approach that accepts limited proprietary components (e.g., NFC on iPhones alongside open alternatives) broadens compatibility and adoption potential, but muddies the independence narrative and complicates certification arguments.
options: Design fallback authentication using only open standards and publicly documented protocols (FIDO2/WebAuthn, OpenID Connect, open-source hardware tokens), explicitly excluding proprietary APIs or platform-specific device-trust signals, accepting narrower short-term adoption in exchange for maximum long-term independence and regulatory clarity.

Develop the fallback with open-standards core but permit optional proprietary integrations (e.g., iOS NFC support, Android secure enclave APIs) for enhanced usability, positioning proprietary features as optional convenience layers rather than trust anchors, risking the perception that true independence is illusory.

Implement the fallback using a hardware-token-first model (FIDO2 keys, smartcards) that bypasses mobile-OS dependency entirely, deferring software-based open-standards authentication to a secondary demonstration phase, reducing scope but narrowing initial target users to security-conscious organizations.
levers.review_lever: Pure open-standards approach is conceptually clean and procurement-friendly but may be perceived as impractical for mass adoption; hybrid approaches increase compatibility but weaken independence claims; hardware-token-first narrows initial scope and adoption but avoids platform-OS dependency friction.

levers.name: Phase-Gate Conditionality: Strict Institutional Traction Versus Schedule-Based Release
levers.consequences: Conditioning phase-two funding release on documented phase-one institutional traction (formal written response from Digitaliseringsstyrelsen, inclusion of neutrality language in an AltID design document, or parliamentary committee endorsement) ensures funding is deployed only when momentum exists, but risks project pause if institutional engagement is slow and may force mid-project scope reduction if conditions are not met. Releasing phase-two funding on schedule regardless of phase-one outcomes preserves team continuity and demonstrator timeline, but may result in demonstrators completed without institutional audience, reducing their leverage and post-completion impact.
options: Condition phase-two release strictly on documented institutional traction by month 8 (formal written response from at least one government authority, or inclusion of platform-neutrality language in a published AltID or related procurement document), pausing or downsizing phase-two if conditions are not met by month 9.

Release phase-two funding on schedule (month 9) regardless of phase-one institutional outcomes, preserving demonstrator development timeline and team stability, accepting the risk that demonstrators may be completed without active institutional sponsorship and require post-hoc positioning.

Hybrid gate: release 60% of phase-two budget in month 9 unconditionally to preserve core demonstrator work, condition the remaining 40% on institutional traction, allowing phase two to proceed with scope flexibility while preserving leverage incentives.
levers.review_lever: Strict institutional gating maximizes leverage but risks project pause if political momentum is delayed; unconditional release preserves timeline but decouples demonstrators from institutional audience; hybrid gating balances continuity with conditionality but requires mid-project budget reallocation and clear scope-reduction criteria.

responses.strategic_rationale: Denmark's digital identity infrastructure faces a critical supplier-concentration risk: MitID's trust model fundamentally depends on Apple and Google platform signals for app integrity, distribution, and device attestation across essential services. The project cannot retrofit MitID itself within its certification constraints, but can establish technical and regulatory groundwork for platform-neutral requirements before AltID hardens identical dependencies. The core tension is between immediate institutional resistance (incumbent operators, platform vendors, and procurement inertia) and long-term resilience: demonstrators must be credible enough to justify procurement language, while coalition and standards pressure must overcome convenience arguments and the appeal of off-the-shelf platform solutions. These seven levers address timing, technical defensibility, institutional leverage, EU alignment, and contingency pathways.

levers.name: Demonstrator Hardware Target: Mobile OS Versus Hardware-Token Isolation
levers.consequences: Choosing GrapheneOS or a comparable privacy-respecting Android builds technical credibility with security experts and standards bodies, but does not eliminate Android OS dependency and may signal an acceptance of open-source mobile platforms rather than true platform-neutrality. A hardware-token demonstrator (USB security key or smartcard) completely sidesteps mobile OS control but introduces usability friction for the majority of citizens and weakens the case that everyday digital access can be made platform-independent without unacceptable burden.
options: Develop both a GrapheneOS-based mobile authenticator and a FIDO2/USB-token fallback demonstrator in parallel, allocating roughly 40% of technical resources to each to ensure both proof-of-concept paths are defensible.

Prioritize a hardware-token and browser-based authentication path as the primary demonstrator, treating GrapheneOS as a secondary exploration, because hardware tokens eliminate OS lock-in entirely and set a harder standard for future procurement language.

Focus exclusively on a GrapheneOS mobile authenticator using open standards, accepting that it trades platform-neutrality for practical usability and making the case that an open-source alternative to iOS/Android fulfills the resilience requirement without separate hardware.
levers.review_lever: Mobile-OS vs. hardware-token framing determines whether demonstrators prove platform-independence (hard requirement) or pragmatic privacy-respecting alternatives (softer claim); conflating them obscures the technical distinction that drives procurement language.

levers.name: Coalition Anchor: Academic Legitimacy Versus Civil-Society Friction
levers.consequences: Leading with university researchers and security experts provides institutional credibility and fends off accusations of ideological or privacy-theater motives; it also aligns the project with Danish research funding and international academic networks. However, academic framing risks sidelining civil-society organizations that have grassroots legitimacy and political pressure capacity, particularly on sovereignty and democratic-accountability angles that resonate in Parliament.
options: Establish the university or research institution as the formal project lead and primary public voice, with civil-society organizations positioned as advisory coalition members, ensuring academic rigor and institutional distance from advocacy.

Co-lead with both an academic researcher and a named civil-society organization (e.g., a privacy advocate or digital-rights group), splitting public representation and media engagement to maintain both technical credibility and grassroots political momentum.

Position civil-society organizations as the formal project convenor, with academic researchers embedded as technical consultants and co-authors, allowing the coalition to leverage existing civil-society networks and political relationships while academics provide credibility on specific claims.
levers.review_lever: Academic-versus-civil-society anchor determines whether the coalition centers institutional credibility (stronger with procurement audiences) or grassroots political pressure (stronger in Parliament and media); choosing wrong weakens engagement with the critical decision-maker.

levers.name: Phase-One Output Sequence: Feasibility Report Timing and Content Lock
levers.consequences: Publishing the feasibility report early (month 5–6) allows coalition messaging and procurement engagement to begin during phase one, but may lock the project into preliminary findings that need revision as technical work deepens. Delaying publication until month 8 accumulates more credible technical detail and allows phase-two demonstrator design to inform recommendations, but compresses the window for institutional influence before phase-two decisions are made.
options: Publish the feasibility report by month 6 with clear caveats and revision markers, treating it as a living document that phase-two technical work updates, to maximize early coalition and policy momentum even at the cost of incomplete technical specification.

Lock the feasibility report at month 8 with full technical detail and demonstrator architecture pre-work, ensuring comprehensive findings and stronger evidentiary weight, accepting that institutional engagement must compress into the final month of phase one.

Release a shorter 'interim policy brief' at month 5, with the full technical feasibility report deferred to month 10 after phase-two demonstrator work has validated key architecture choices, splitting the messaging burden and allowing two engagement windows.
levers.review_lever: Early publication builds coalition momentum but risks incomplete technical grounding; delayed publication strengthens evidence but compresses phase-one advocacy into a single month and leaves AltID procurement on a faster timeline.

levers.name: MitID Operator Engagement: Formal Negotiation Versus External Standards Pressure
levers.consequences: Direct engagement with the MitID operator (and its parent authority) risks being perceived as inside lobbying and may trigger organizational defensiveness around their current architecture and vendor relationships. External standards pressure via EU bodies and procurement language allows the project to influence outcomes without direct confrontation, but leaves the MitID operator free to ignore platform-neutrality arguments if they can absorb or deflect them through existing regulatory compliance.
options: Initiate formal documented engagement with the MitID operator and Digitaliseringsstyrelsen in phase one, presenting the feasibility report and fallback-authentication concept as collaborative input for AltID design, accepting the risk of organizational pushback or co-option.

Avoid direct MitID operator engagement in phases one and two, instead building coalition, standards input, and procurement language, then present the demonstrators and EU alignment outcomes to the operator and authority only at the start of phase three as fait accompli technical evidence.

Conduct a single structured 'stakeholder validation workshop' with the MitID operator and other authorities in month 7, framed as seeking feedback on technical feasibility rather than policy pressure, to maintain communication while avoiding premature commitment or defensive reactions.
levers.review_lever: Direct negotiation with the operator offers insider influence but risks defensive institutional resistance; external standards pressure scales horizontally across EU but leaves the operator room to ignore or marginalize platform-neutrality demands.

levers.name: EU Standards Engagement Scope: Bilateral Versus Consortium-Based
levers.consequences: Bilateral engagement with relevant European Digital Identity Wallet working groups allows the project to tailor messaging to specific EU technical and policy priorities, but depends on the project's limited diplomatic capacity and may not survive institutional turnover at the EU level. Joining or co-founding a multi-country consortium (with other Nordic or EU countries also concerned about platform dependency) multiplies credibility and political weight, but requires months of coordination negotiation and dilutes the project's core influence over final language.
options: Conduct direct bilateral outreach to the European Digital Identity Wallet technical working groups, the eIDAS2 implementation taskforce, and relevant NIST or ETSI standardization bodies, submitting the feasibility report and demonstrators as technical input with Denmark as a named contributing state.

Initiate a Nordic coalition with Sweden, Norway, and possibly Estonia (all facing similar platform-dependency risks) to jointly propose platform-neutrality and fallback-access requirements to EU bodies, multiplying political leverage but requiring lead-time coordination before phase two.

Contribute the project's findings to an existing multi-stakeholder digital-identity initiative (e.g., EUDIW, DSSC) rather than founding a new coalition, accepting diffuse influence in exchange for faster institutional access and established forums without coordination overhead.
levers.review_lever: Bilateral EU engagement offers tactical speed but fragile influence; consortium approaches multiply political weight but consume lead time and dilute the project's specific framing of platform-dependency risk as a Danish and Northern European concern.

levers.name: Financing Continuity Contingency: Multi-Funder Diversification Versus Single-Sponsor Concentration
levers.consequences: Securing phase-two and phase-three funding from a single government ministry or program (e.g., Digitaliseringsstyrelsen's budget) streamlines approvals and accountability but creates existential risk if that ministry's priorities shift, budgets are frozen, or political leadership changes. Diversifying funding across a foundation, EU research grant, and government co-funding spreads risk but requires writing multiple proposals in parallel and managing conflicting funder reporting requirements and timelines.
options: Establish a primary funding relationship with Digitaliseringsstyrelsen or a related government entity as the formal phase-gate sponsor, with any supplementary funding (e.g., Carlsberg Foundation or EU research grants) treated as secondary top-ups, accepting single-sponsor concentration risk for streamlined governance.

Pursue parallel funding proposals to three distinct sources (a government ministry, a Danish foundation focused on digital resilience or democracy, and an EU Horizon or DIGITAL programme grant) with a target of covering 50–60% of each phase from at least two sources, prioritizing funding independence over administrative simplicity.

Secure a commitment from the Danish state for core operating costs (salaries, workspace) while treating discrete demonstrator and external-review work as competitive grant opportunities, maintaining government relationship as the backbone while diversifying project-specific spending.
levers.review_lever: Single-funder concentration provides streamlined approval but creates fragility if priorities shift; multi-source diversification protects against cancellation but multiplies compliance burden and creates timeline misalignment between funder reporting cycles.

levers.name: Fallback Access Governance Model: Standards-Mandated Versus Procurement-Soft-Requirement
levers.consequences: Embedding fallback-access requirements into eIDAS2 or NSIS standards forces all member states' identity systems to implement platform-neutral pathways, but requires formal EU legislative or standardization action that may take years and faces vendor lobbying. Proposing fallback access as a soft procurement requirement in Danish AltID documentation (best-practice language rather than hard mandate) can be adopted faster and allows vendors flexibility to innovate, but provides no guarantee that future operators will maintain the fallback path or invest in its usability.
options: Push for formal inclusion of platform-neutrality and fallback-access requirements in eIDAS2 implementing acts or relevant ETSI standards, recognizing this requires EU-level advocacy and multi-year timelines but creates durable, legally enforceable obligations across all member states.

Propose platform-neutrality and fallback-access as 'mandatory technical considerations' in Danish procurement for AltID and related identity systems, allowing vendors to meet requirements through various technical approaches while avoiding formal standards lock-in and enabling pragmatic flexibility.

Establish a voluntary 'Danish Digital Identity Resilience Charter' signed by Digitaliseringsstyrelsen, the MitID operator, and major public-sector service providers, committing to platform-neutral architecture and fallback access as operational targets without legal enforcement, relying on reputational and political pressure to maintain compliance.
levers.review_lever: Standards-mandated requirements are durable but face years of EU negotiation and vendor resistance; procurement soft requirements are faster to adopt but non-binding and vulnerable to deprioritization once demonstrators fade from institutional attention.

levers.name: Demonstrator Scope and Fidelity
levers.consequences: Building working (but non-production) authenticators using FIDO2 and OpenID Connect on GrapheneOS proves that secure, standards-based, Apple/Google-independent authentication is technically feasible without requiring proprietary platform APIs. This lowers the perceived risk for procurement officials and standards bodies considering fallback requirements. The trade-off is that demonstrators do not integrate with live MitID or real public-sector identity providers, so they do not prove end-to-end operational compatibility or resolve all integration friction that would emerge at scale.
options: Develop two parallel demonstrators: one mobile-oriented (GrapheneOS or comparable platform running FIDO2/OpenID Connect) and one browser-based or hardware-token-based path that eliminates mobile-OS dependency altogether, each authenticated against a simulated Danish public-sector identity environment with published architecture documentation.

Focus demonstrator effort on a single, heavily polished mobile authenticator running on GrapheneOS that closely mirrors MitID's user interaction model and security posture, aiming for near-production-grade code quality and formal security review to maximize institutional credibility.

Pursue a lightweight proof-of-concept using existing open-source authentication libraries (e.g., Keycloak with FIDO2 modules) integrated with a mock identity provider, prioritizing speed to demonstration over custom development and accepting lower fidelity in exchange for faster iteration and lower technical risk.
levers.review: A more sophisticated demonstrator improves institutional buy-in but risks scope creep and diverts engineering effort from policy leverage; a minimal proof-of-concept spreads resources thinly across coalition-building but may be dismissed as too academic or immature for procurement relevance.

levers.name: Institutional Entry Point and Engagement Strategy
levers.consequences: Engaging formally with Digitaliseringsstyrelsen, the MitID operator, or a regulatory body creates a documented commitment point and forces officials to provide written responses that either endorse platform-neutral requirements or articulate explicit resistance (which the project can then address). Early formal engagement builds credibility and creates institutional friction against backsliding. The risk is that incumbent operators or existing MitID stakeholders may actively undermine the project or lobby against platform-neutrality language, and early engagement can also prompt defensive institutional posturing if framed as a direct threat to existing investments.
options: Target Digitaliseringsstyrelsen directly with a formal written proposal framed around digital sovereignty and procurement neutrality, requesting an official steering-committee role or monthly update briefing to ensure the project shapes AltID design from the inside rather than remaining external pressure.

Approach the Danish Data Protection Authority (Datatilsynet) with a request for a public statement on platform-neutrality and fallback-access implications for data minimization and GDPR compliance, using privacy framing to create institutional pressure that does not directly threaten the MitID operator.

Engage with a sympathetic municipality or regional health authority using demonstrators to pilot a fallback-capable authentication interface, creating operational proof and local political pressure for platform-neutral procurement requirements in subsequent contracts.
levers.review: Direct steering-committee placement risks co-option or blocking by incumbents; privacy-authority framing deprioritizes resilience and sovereignty arguments; municipal pilots build bottom-up pressure but move slowly and may lack influence on national AltID architecture decisions.

levers.name: Coalition Composition and Messaging
levers.consequences: A coalition spanning civil-society organisations, privacy advocates, academic researchers, security experts, and sympathetic parliamentarians creates distributed political and institutional pressure that cannot be easily dismissed as a single vendor's interests or an ideological fringe position. Different coalition members amplify different messages: security researchers emphasize technical feasibility, privacy groups emphasize data minimization and democratic accountability, and continuity-planning stakeholders emphasize resilience and supplier concentration risk. The challenge is that coalitions dilute focus and can become platforms for diverse agendas that weaken the core message around platform neutrality and fallback access.
options: Build a broad coalition including civil-society organisations, academic institutions, and EU-facing standards bodies (e.g., ETSI working groups), with explicit messaging discipline ensuring all members emphasize digital sovereignty, resilience, and reduced supplier concentration as primary drivers rather than secondary privacy or ideological concerns.

Form a narrower, technically credible coalition of security researchers and compliance experts with direct links to academic and industry standards bodies, positioning the project as a technical standards initiative rather than a political movement and accepting lower civil-society visibility in exchange for institutional weight.

Develop separate, audience-specific coalitions: a technical working group for standards bodies and procurement officials, a privacy-and-democracy coalition for civil-society and media engagement, and a parliamentary task force for political leverage, each with distinct messaging tailored to institutional incentives and risk tolerances.
levers.review: Broad coalition maximizes political pressure but risks diluted messaging and slower consensus-building; narrow technical credibility improves standards traction but limits political cover if incumbents attack the project; segmented coalitions require sustained coordination overhead and may create contradictory external narratives.

levers.name: Feasibility Report Content and Publication Strategy
levers.consequences: A published feasibility and risk report that maps MitID dependencies, articulates platform-neutrality and fallback-access architecture options, and documents regulatory pathways under eIDAS2 and NSIS creates a citable reference document that procurement officials and standards bodies must address explicitly rather than ignore. Publication also distributes the project's analysis across European digital identity policy networks, raising the cost of dismissing supplier-concentration concerns as purely Danish or ideologically motivated. The trade-off is that a detailed technical report requires significant research and external review investment, and early publication may prompt defensive responses or lobbying from incumbent operators that accelerate opposition rather than convert skeptics.
options: Publish a comprehensive, externally reviewed feasibility and risk report (80–120 pages) covering architectural options, regulatory compliance pathways, supplier-concentration risks, and implementation timelines, with formal launch events at Digitaliseringsstyrelsen, EU technical working groups, and academic conferences to maximize institutional and media visibility.

Release a shorter, more accessible policy brief (15–25 pages) targeting procurement officials and parliamentarians, with detailed technical annexes available separately, prioritizing clarity and decision-maker accessibility over exhaustive coverage and aiming for faster dissemination and lower incumbent resistance.

Publish findings incrementally through academic conferences, EU standards working groups, and policy journals rather than a single consolidated report, spreading impact over time and reducing the visibility of a single confrontational document while allowing continuous refinement based on feedback.
levers.review: Comprehensive publication maximizes institutional impact and creates a hard policy reference point, but also invites consolidated incumbent criticism and raises visibility to potential blockers; shorter briefs improve stakeholder accessibility but may be dismissed as insufficiently rigorous; incremental publication spreads impact but risks losing the coherence needed for procurement language adoption.

levers.name: EU-Level Standards Alignment and Negotiation
levers.consequences: Positioning Danish platform-neutrality and fallback-access arguments within the broader European Digital Identity Wallet (EUDI Wallet) framework and relevant eIDAS2 technical working groups anchors the project in supranational compliance and interoperability mandates rather than framing it as a Danish national preference. This creates pressure on Danish authorities to adopt requirements that align with EU-wide standards, reducing the risk that the project is dismissed as isolated or unilateral. The challenge is that EU-level engagement moves slowly, requires sustained diplomatic effort, and may be weakened by other Member States prioritizing incumbent operators or interoperability with existing national stacks.
options: Engage directly with ETSI, the EUDI Wallet technical working groups, and the European Commission's digital identity coordination structures to propose language supporting platform-neutral access and certified fallback mechanisms, positioning these as requirements for EU wallet interoperability rather than Danish-specific preferences.

Coordinate with sympathetic European Member States (e.g., Estonia, Netherlands) that share digital-sovereignty concerns to develop joint position papers and standards proposals, creating a broader coalition that makes dismissing platform-neutrality concerns harder for the Commission or other Member States.

Support the emergence of an independent European standards body or open-source authentication initiative that defines platform-neutral identity specifications, with Danish project demonstrators contributing proof-of-concept code and regulatory feedback to establish credible alternatives to Apple/Google-centric models.
levers.review: Direct engagement with EU bodies improves long-term legitimacy but offers no guarantee of rapid policy change and may be viewed as premature by Danish stakeholders; multi-country coalitions amplify pressure but reduce Danish control over messaging; independent open-source standards bodies build technical credibility but take years to achieve institutional recognition.

levers.name: Fallback Access Path Definition and Use-Case Binding
levers.consequences: Defining a concrete, use-case-specific fallback authentication path (e.g., hardware-token-based, browser-based, or otherwise OS-agnostic) tied to critical services such as tax filing, healthcare access, or social-security claims demonstrates that resilience is not abstract but operationally necessary. This makes fallback access requirements harder to dismiss as optional or ideological. Defining use cases also forces procurement and architecture conversations to address what continuity of service actually means and what happens if the primary mobile-OS-dependent path fails. The trade-off is that narrowing fallback design to specific use cases reduces the universality of the solution and may invite incumbent pushback that fallback mechanisms should only apply to edge cases or geographic exceptions rather than core architectural requirements.
options: Specify a hardware-security-token-based fallback path (e.g., FIDO2-compatible USB or NFC tokens) usable for high-assurance transactions such as healthcare access and tax filing, ensuring it functions across all operating systems and does not depend on app-store distribution or platform integrity APIs.

Define a browser-based fallback using open standards (OpenID Connect with FIDO2 discoverable credentials) accessible from any device with a modern web browser, allowing citizens without specific mobile platforms to authenticate to public services without needing an iOS or Android app at all.

Establish a tiered resilience model where routine services rely on the current mobile-OS-dependent primary path, critical or time-sensitive services (emergency healthcare, benefits claims) trigger automatic fallback to a browser or hardware-token mechanism, and this tiering is formalized in AltID procurement and operational requirements.
levers.review: Hardware tokens ensure OS independence but add cost, distribution burden, and user friction that may limit adoption; browser-based fallback reduces friction but may be perceived as lower-assurance and may struggle to achieve equivalent regulatory recognition; tiered resilience adds complexity to system design and procurement language but directly ties fallback mechanisms to demonstrated operational risk.

levers.name: Financing and Phase-Gate Risk Management
levers.consequences: Structuring the project into three phases with conditional funding (phases 2 and 3 contingent on phase 1 deliverables) ensures that the project does not commit large resources to downstream work if early institutional engagement fails or if the feasibility report reveals insurmountable blockers. This also creates natural decision points where the project can pivot toward EU-level standards input or coalition consolidation if Danish procurement leverage is weak. The challenge is that conditional funding creates uncertainty for the team, may discourage long-term staffing commitments, and may cause the project to lose momentum or miss windows of opportunity if phase gates are triggered before stakeholder engagement is sufficient.
options: Commit to full 10.5-million-DKK funding across all three phases upfront, treating phase gates as strategic checkpoints rather than hard funding barriers, ensuring team stability and allowing the project to pursue multiple intervention pathways simultaneously without artificial phase constraints interrupting momentum.

Implement strict phase-gate funding with transparent, publicly documented decision criteria, so that if phase 2 is not triggered due to insufficient institutional engagement, the project formally shifts to EU-level standards contribution and coalition consolidation, treating the strategic pivot as an acceptable outcome rather than a failure.

Secure parallel funding streams from EU digital-identity research programs, academic institutions, or civil-society networks, reducing dependence on the initial 10.5-million-DKK allocation and allowing phases to progress in parallel with lower inter-phase financial dependency.
levers.review: Full upfront funding ensures team continuity but may waste resources if Danish procurement leverage does not materialize; strict phase gating enforces disciplined strategy but may trigger abandonment of Danish advocacy if metrics are met too early; parallel funding reduces risk but complicates governance and may dilute focus across multiple funders' priorities.

levers.name: Demonstrator Positioning: Technical Proof Versus Political Signal
levers.consequences: Positioning the mobile and fallback demonstrators as narrow, non-production feasibility proofs rather than feature-complete alternatives reduces development scope and credibility risk, but may undermine their persuasiveness to procurement officials who expect to see operational maturity. Conversely, expanding them toward production readiness inflates budget, timeline, and certification complexity, potentially consuming the entire phase-two budget without achieving the advocacy goal.
options: Build minimal demonstrators (GrapheneOS + FIDO2 and a browser-based token fallback) deliberately constrained to three core authentication flows, with explicit documentation of what is intentionally omitted to remain within phase-two scope and budget.

Develop demonstrators with partial feature parity to MitID (multi-factor recovery, account linking, audit logging) to increase perceived credibility among technical reviewers, accepting a 15–20% budget increase and delayed delivery risk.

Partner with an existing open-source mobile identity project (e.g., a European eID wallet initiative) and contribute fallback-authentication modules rather than building demonstrators in-house, reducing isolation risk but accepting dependency on external project roadmaps.
levers.review: Minimal scope preserves budget and timeline credibility, but narrow demonstrators may be dismissed as toys rather than evidence; feature expansion risks scope creep and budget overrun without guaranteeing procurement influence.

levers.name: Coalition Anchor Selection: Which Authority to Target First
levers.consequences: Early formal engagement with one sympathetic authority (e.g., the Data Protection Board or a parliamentary digital-policy committee member) creates institutional validation and media narrative momentum, but risks signaling a political stance that alienates other potential allies or triggers preemptive resistance from MitID operators. Sequencing toward multiple modest stakeholders instead spreads attention and reduces accusation of partisan coordination, but delays high-visibility wins and may dilute message clarity.
options: Target a single respected authority (e.g., the Datatilsynet or a senior Folketinget digital-policy member) for an early, publicly announced formal response or endorsement, accepting the political concentration risk in exchange for clear narrative momentum.

Build a broad coalition across civil-society organizations, academic institutions, and regional government bodies first, then present a collective position to Digitaliseringsstyrelsen, ensuring distributed legitimacy but delaying visible institutional traction until month 12–14.

Approach the MitID operator directly with a confidential proposal to collaborate on fallback pathways, framing it as strategic partnership rather than criticism, risking co-option but potentially converting the incumbent into a neutral or supportive voice.
levers.review: Early single-authority wins create narrative credibility but concentrate political exposure; broad coalition building delays visible traction but disperses risk and reduces accusation of partisan pressure or incumbent capture.

levers.name: Resilience Framing Versus Sovereignty Language in Policy Messaging
levers.consequences: Emphasizing continuity-of-service, supplier-concentration, and contingency risk ('What if Apple or Google withdraw from Denmark?') appeals to risk managers and procurement officers but risks being perceived as alarmist or commercially motivated if competitors are suspected of backing the messaging. Framing as digital sovereignty and democratic control attracts civil-society and parliamentary support but triggers incumbent framing of the concern as ideological and expensive, and may activate EU-level free-trade sensitivities.
options: Lead messaging with resilience, contingency, and supplier-concentration risk (suppliers cannot simultaneously leave or be locked by geopolitical pressure), positioning fallback access as critical infrastructure continuity planning, de-emphasizing ideology.

Anchor messaging in democratic sovereignty and reduced dependence on foreign tech-platform policy decisions that affect Danish public-sector autonomy, accepting that this framing will trigger incumbent claims of expense and unrealism.

Dual-track messaging: resilience and contingency planning in procurement and risk-management forums; sovereignty and democratic control in parliamentary and civil-society contexts, with a unified technical brief explaining both framings as complementary rather than contradictory.
levers.review: Resilience framing is operationally credible but may be dismissed as overblown; sovereignty framing mobilizes civil society but invites dismissal as ideologically driven; dual-track messaging increases coordination overhead and risks internal contradiction if not carefully managed.

levers.name: Stakeholder Sequencing: Sympathetic-First Versus Incumbent-Negotiation Approach
levers.consequences: Building momentum through early wins with sympathetic civil-society, academic, and parliamentary allies before formally engaging MitID operators or Digitaliseringsstyrelsen creates political weight and precedent, but risks being perceived as a coordinated campaign to exclude incumbents, triggering defensive mobilization and procurement delays. Direct early engagement with operators shows good faith and may uncover technical collaboration opportunities, but dilutes pressure and may result in assurances that deflect policy change without substantive action.
options: Secure published support from at least three independent civil-society and academic organizations and one parliamentary ally by month 6, establish the fallback-access concept in public discourse, then approach Digitaliseringsstyrelsen and the MitID operator from a position of demonstrated coalition strength.

Request formal technical working-group participation with the MitID operator and Digitaliseringsstyrelsen by month 3, treating them as co-designers rather than obstacles, accepting slower narrative momentum in exchange for insider access and potential collaborative problem-solving.

Parallel-path approach: simultaneously build civil-society coalition and initiate low-key technical discussions with sympathetic officials within Digitaliseringsstyrelsen or AltID governance, avoiding public confrontation until month 12 when demonstrators and coalition provide joint credibility.
levers.review: Sympathetic-first approach builds political power but risks appearing coordinated or exclusionary; incumbent-first risks co-option or capture; parallel-path spreads resources and requires careful message discipline to avoid appearing duplicitous.

levers.name: EU-Level Standards Engagement Scope: Domestic Leverage Versus European Alignment
levers.consequences: Deep early engagement with European Digital Identity Wallet working groups and eIDAS2 implementation bodies amplifies the project's reach and aligns Danish advocacy with broader EU momentum on interoperability and resilience, but may slow phase-three domestic procurement impact if European alignment requires consensus-building across member states with different vendor relationships. Focusing first on Danish AltID procurement and then scaling to EU standards bodies preserves domestic momentum but risks missing the window for European-level language if eIDAS2 wallet implementation timelines are already set.
options: Engage with relevant EU technical working groups (eIDAS2 Wallet rollout, NSIS implementation) by month 8, propose platform-neutrality and fallback-access requirements at the EU level, positioning Denmark as a leader in resilience standards, accepting slower domestic impact if European buy-in is delayed.

Concentrate phase-three effort on AltID and Danish procurement language, treating EU engagement as secondary and deferred to month 18–20, preserving focus and budget for domestic institutional traction but risking missed leverage if European timelines accelerate.

Dual-track EU engagement: observe and participate in standards discussions from month 6 onward (low-intensity), then escalate to formal position papers and procurement-language proposals by month 14 once demonstrators and Danish institutional traction are visible, balancing European alignment with domestic credibility.
levers.review: Early deep EU engagement amplifies reach but may slow domestic wins; domestic-first focus preserves clarity but risks European window closure; dual-track requires sustained coordination and risks appearing reactive at both levels if timing misaligns.

levers.name: Fallback-Access Design Governance: Standards-Based Versus Proprietary-Hybrid
levers.consequences: Committing the fallback demonstrator entirely to open standards (WebAuthn, OpenID Connect, FIDO2, hardware tokens) maximizes platform independence and procurement appeal, but reduces integration options with existing MitID infrastructure and may exclude approaches that leverage proprietary device-security features without full Apple/Google mediation. A hybrid approach that accepts limited proprietary components (e.g., NFC on iPhones alongside open alternatives) broadens compatibility and adoption potential, but muddies the independence narrative and complicates certification arguments.
options: Design fallback authentication using only open standards and publicly documented protocols (FIDO2/WebAuthn, OpenID Connect, open-source hardware tokens), explicitly excluding proprietary APIs or platform-specific device-trust signals, accepting narrower short-term adoption in exchange for maximum long-term independence and regulatory clarity.

Develop the fallback with open-standards core but permit optional proprietary integrations (e.g., iOS NFC support, Android secure enclave APIs) for enhanced usability, positioning proprietary features as optional convenience layers rather than trust anchors, risking the perception that true independence is illusory.

Implement the fallback using a hardware-token-first model (FIDO2 keys, smartcards) that bypasses mobile-OS dependency entirely, deferring software-based open-standards authentication to a secondary demonstration phase, reducing scope but narrowing initial target users to security-conscious organizations.
levers.review: Pure open-standards approach is conceptually clean and procurement-friendly but may be perceived as impractical for mass adoption; hybrid approaches increase compatibility but weaken independence claims; hardware-token-first narrows initial scope and adoption but avoids platform-OS dependency friction.

levers.name: Phase-Gate Conditionality: Strict Institutional Traction Versus Schedule-Based Release
levers.consequences: Conditioning phase-two funding release on documented phase-one institutional traction (formal written response from Digitaliseringsstyrelsen, inclusion of neutrality language in an AltID design document, or parliamentary committee endorsement) ensures funding is deployed only when momentum exists, but risks project pause if institutional engagement is slow and may force mid-project scope reduction if conditions are not met. Releasing phase-two funding on schedule regardless of phase-one outcomes preserves team continuity and demonstrator timeline, but may result in demonstrators completed without institutional audience, reducing their leverage and post-completion impact.
options: Condition phase-two release strictly on documented institutional traction by month 8 (formal written response from at least one government authority, or inclusion of platform-neutrality language in a published AltID or related procurement document), pausing or downsizing phase-two if conditions are not met by month 9.

Release phase-two funding on schedule (month 9) regardless of phase-one institutional outcomes, preserving demonstrator development timeline and team stability, accepting the risk that demonstrators may be completed without active institutional sponsorship and require post-hoc positioning.

Hybrid gate: release 60% of phase-two budget in month 9 unconditionally to preserve core demonstrator work, condition the remaining 40% on institutional traction, allowing phase two to proceed with scope flexibility while preserving leverage incentives.
levers.review: Strict institutional gating maximizes leverage but risks project pause if political momentum is delayed; unconditional release preserves timeline but decouples demonstrators from institutional audience; hybrid gating balances continuity with conditionality but requires mid-project budget reallocation and clear scope-reduction criteria.

levers.name: Demonstrator Hardware Target: Mobile OS Versus Hardware-Token Isolation
levers.consequences: Choosing GrapheneOS or a comparable privacy-respecting Android builds technical credibility with security experts and standards bodies, but does not eliminate Android OS dependency and may signal an acceptance of open-source mobile platforms rather than true platform-neutrality. A hardware-token demonstrator (USB security key or smartcard) completely sidesteps mobile OS control but introduces usability friction for the majority of citizens and weakens the case that everyday digital access can be made platform-independent without unacceptable burden.
options: Develop both a GrapheneOS-based mobile authenticator and a FIDO2/USB-token fallback demonstrator in parallel, allocating roughly 40% of technical resources to each to ensure both proof-of-concept paths are defensible.

Prioritize a hardware-token and browser-based authentication path as the primary demonstrator, treating GrapheneOS as a secondary exploration, because hardware tokens eliminate OS lock-in entirely and set a harder standard for future procurement language.

Focus exclusively on a GrapheneOS mobile authenticator using open standards, accepting that it trades platform-neutrality for practical usability and making the case that an open-source alternative to iOS/Android fulfills the resilience requirement without separate hardware.
levers.review: Mobile-OS vs. hardware-token framing determines whether demonstrators prove platform-independence (hard requirement) or pragmatic privacy-respecting alternatives (softer claim); conflating them obscures the technical distinction that drives procurement language.

levers.name: Coalition Anchor: Academic Legitimacy Versus Civil-Society Friction
levers.consequences: Leading with university researchers and security experts provides institutional credibility and fends off accusations of ideological or privacy-theater motives; it also aligns the project with Danish research funding and international academic networks. However, academic framing risks sidelining civil-society organizations that have grassroots legitimacy and political pressure capacity, particularly on sovereignty and democratic-accountability angles that resonate in Parliament.
options: Establish the university or research institution as the formal project lead and primary public voice, with civil-society organizations positioned as advisory coalition members, ensuring academic rigor and institutional distance from advocacy.

Co-lead with both an academic researcher and a named civil-society organization (e.g., a privacy advocate or digital-rights group), splitting public representation and media engagement to maintain both technical credibility and grassroots political momentum.

Position civil-society organizations as the formal project convenor, with academic researchers embedded as technical consultants and co-authors, allowing the coalition to leverage existing civil-society networks and political relationships while academics provide credibility on specific claims.
levers.review: Academic-versus-civil-society anchor determines whether the coalition centers institutional credibility (stronger with procurement audiences) or grassroots political pressure (stronger in Parliament and media); choosing wrong weakens engagement with the critical decision-maker.

levers.name: Phase-One Output Sequence: Feasibility Report Timing and Content Lock
levers.consequences: Publishing the feasibility report early (month 5–6) allows coalition messaging and procurement engagement to begin during phase one, but may lock the project into preliminary findings that need revision as technical work deepens. Delaying publication until month 8 accumulates more credible technical detail and allows phase-two demonstrator design to inform recommendations, but compresses the window for institutional influence before phase-two decisions are made.
options: Publish the feasibility report by month 6 with clear caveats and revision markers, treating it as a living document that phase-two technical work updates, to maximize early coalition and policy momentum even at the cost of incomplete technical specification.

Lock the feasibility report at month 8 with full technical detail and demonstrator architecture pre-work, ensuring comprehensive findings and stronger evidentiary weight, accepting that institutional engagement must compress into the final month of phase one.

Release a shorter 'interim policy brief' at month 5, with the full technical feasibility report deferred to month 10 after phase-two demonstrator work has validated key architecture choices, splitting the messaging burden and allowing two engagement windows.
levers.review: Early publication builds coalition momentum but risks incomplete technical grounding; delayed publication strengthens evidence but compresses phase-one advocacy into a single month and leaves AltID procurement on a faster timeline.

levers.name: MitID Operator Engagement: Formal Negotiation Versus External Standards Pressure
levers.consequences: Direct engagement with the MitID operator (and its parent authority) risks being perceived as inside lobbying and may trigger organizational defensiveness around their current architecture and vendor relationships. External standards pressure via EU bodies and procurement language allows the project to influence outcomes without direct confrontation, but leaves the MitID operator free to ignore platform-neutrality arguments if they can absorb or deflect them through existing regulatory compliance.
options: Initiate formal documented engagement with the MitID operator and Digitaliseringsstyrelsen in phase one, presenting the feasibility report and fallback-authentication concept as collaborative input for AltID design, accepting the risk of organizational pushback or co-option.

Avoid direct MitID operator engagement in phases one and two, instead building coalition, standards input, and procurement language, then present the demonstrators and EU alignment outcomes to the operator and authority only at the start of phase three as fait accompli technical evidence.

Conduct a single structured 'stakeholder validation workshop' with the MitID operator and other authorities in month 7, framed as seeking feedback on technical feasibility rather than policy pressure, to maintain communication while avoiding premature commitment or defensive reactions.
levers.review: Direct negotiation with the operator offers insider influence but risks defensive institutional resistance; external standards pressure scales horizontally across EU but leaves the operator room to ignore or marginalize platform-neutrality demands.

levers.name: EU Standards Engagement Scope: Bilateral Versus Consortium-Based
levers.consequences: Bilateral engagement with relevant European Digital Identity Wallet working groups allows the project to tailor messaging to specific EU technical and policy priorities, but depends on the project's limited diplomatic capacity and may not survive institutional turnover at the EU level. Joining or co-founding a multi-country consortium (with other Nordic or EU countries also concerned about platform dependency) multiplies credibility and political weight, but requires months of coordination negotiation and dilutes the project's core influence over final language.
options: Conduct direct bilateral outreach to the European Digital Identity Wallet technical working groups, the eIDAS2 implementation taskforce, and relevant NIST or ETSI standardization bodies, submitting the feasibility report and demonstrators as technical input with Denmark as a named contributing state.

Initiate a Nordic coalition with Sweden, Norway, and possibly Estonia (all facing similar platform-dependency risks) to jointly propose platform-neutrality and fallback-access requirements to EU bodies, multiplying political leverage but requiring lead-time coordination before phase two.

Contribute the project's findings to an existing multi-stakeholder digital-identity initiative (e.g., EUDIW, DSSC) rather than founding a new coalition, accepting diffuse influence in exchange for faster institutional access and established forums without coordination overhead.
levers.review: Bilateral EU engagement offers tactical speed but fragile influence; consortium approaches multiply political weight but consume lead time and dilute the project's specific framing of platform-dependency risk as a Danish and Northern European concern.
